extraction.research_question: No explicit research question. The document describes and documents the LobbyView database, which links congressional bill sponsorship with lobbying reports filed under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995, and the API used to bulk-download it (Abstract; Section 1).
extraction.theory: No theory section. The Abstract gives the motivation only: lobbying by special interest groups matters for policymaking, and empirical studies of political representation have been limited by the difficulty of observing a direct link between politicians and interest groups.
extraction.data: Source: the universe of lobbying reports filed under the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 (Abstract). Units named in the text: lobbying reports, lobbying issue sections ("specific issues"), bills (ids of the form "110_HR7311", Section 5.2), firms/clients, and industries (NAICS2 groupings, Section 5.5). Sample size N: not reported. Time period: not stated as a single range; the CONGRESSES setting in general.py sets the range and its default values are not given (Section 4.1). Example years used in the text are illustrative (2002 Mattel report, 2011 filter example, 2013 Google report). Firm financials come from Compustat (Section 5.5.2), and industry codes from NAICS and SIC. The 52,418 count in Section 5.3 is a query result over all loaded reports that carry the TRADE (DOMESTIC/FOREIGN) issue; the text gives no year restriction for it.
extraction.method: Descriptive data construction, not statistical estimation. Bills in reports are found by regular-expression search for bill numbers (Section 2, step 1). The Congress is assigned by maximizing the cosine similarity between a bag-of-words vector of each candidate bill and a vector of the text around the bill mention, over the candidate Congresses (Section 2, step 2, Eq. 1). Congress numbers propagate across a report, with majority vote where bills disagree (step 3). Bill titles are matched to report text (step 4). Bill ranges are expanded (step 5). Storage uses SQLite with SQLAlchemy and Elixir, and full-text search uses Whoosh over CRS summaries and specific issues (Sections 3.1, 5.4). Herfindahl indices are computed per industry (herfindahl.py), then augmented with a trade-issue indicator and Compustat data (herfindadd.py) (Section 5.5).
extraction.identification: None. The paper makes no causal claim and presents no identification strategy.
extraction.scope: Population: lobbying reports and firms/clients under the LDA (1995 onward). Institution: US Congress bills and their sponsorship. Era: post-1995 LDA filings, with the Congress range set in configuration. Stated purpose: enable systematic research on lobbying and merging with external datasets (Abstract).

summary_md:
Kim's 2018 LobbyView note is a partial technical manual, not an empirical study. It has no estimates, no N and no stated coverage window. It documents how LDA lobbying reports get linked to congressional bills. First, a regex finds bill numbers. Then each mention is assigned to a Congress by taking the argmax of cosine similarity between the candidate bill text and the text around the mention, looking back three Congresses by default; if nothing matches, the code falls back to the filing-year Congress. The Congress is then propagated across the report by majority vote, titles are matched, and close bill numbers (gap of 10 or less) are expanded into ranges. Industries are grouped by NAICS2/SIC for per-industry Herfindahl indices, with Compustat merged in. The note names one failure case: Google's 2013 report cites H.R. 2577, which is a 112th-Congress bill, so the naive filing-year rule gets it wrong. It gives no error rates for any heuristic.

This matters for Paul's lobbying lane in three ways:
1. **Every LobbyView-derived member link is a bill-roster join, not a contact record.** That backs the system's finding that the lobbied-member link is circular.
2. **Paul's own LDA rebuild uses a different bill-resolution rule than the LobbyView pipeline.** A citation without an "of 20XX" suffix binds to the filing-year Congress, which is the naive rule this paper says fails. Hyphenated ranges are not expanded. So the network.csv vintage (2000-2022) and the 2021+ rebuild are different instruments with an unmeasured seam between them.
3. **The paper uses NAICS as an industry grouping.** The system has ruled NAICS to be linkage metadata only.

None of this is a validation of anything. The heuristics' accuracy is unreported, and the argmax always returns an answer.

gaps_exposed: The 2021+ LDA rebuild has no prior-Congress lookback for unsuffixed bill citations. They bind to the filing Congress, which is the failure case the paper documents (H.R. 2577, 112th Congress, cited in a 2013 report). The system has never measured how often this happens in the finance rebuild.

No overlap-year (2021) reconciliation between LobbyView network.csv dyads and the system's strict rebuild was found in the notes I read. A future bridge successor would cross an unmeasured instrument seam (UNVERIFIED).
The paper reports no error rates for any linkage heuristic. Both instruments, LobbyView and the rebuild, lack a hand-labelled precision/recall sample for bill-to-Congress resolution.
flags: The paper describes the link as bill 'sponsorship', but the system measured that LobbyView network edges are the sponsor plus all cosponsors. Any wording that inherits the paper's description understates the join and should say 'sponsored or cosponsored'.

D-021: the paper's design turns lobbying reports into member-linked edges and industry Herfindahl weights. Adopting either as an edge or weight source in the Melange graphs would conflict with D-021, which allows LDA as an identity source only (lob_id, client names).
Nothing in the paper licenses influence or contact language about lobbied members. The link is a bill-roster join, so P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction.
The 52,418 TRADE-issue report count has no window or year restriction in the text. It must not be quoted without stating that it covers 'all loaded reports, period unstated'.

The paper's argmax-plus-fallback Congress assignment always returns an answer. Copying it as-is would break the system's never-guess, fail-closed resolution style. Any adoption should flag ambiguous citations instead.
paul_alignment: The paper agrees with Paul's annotation, which cites it only in the contact-inference memos as a cautionary chain where an argmax always returns an answer. His broader position that LobbyView is the 'fundamental data source' for lobbying classification is stale against the system now, for three reasons. First, the system found that LobbyView NAICS is linkage metadata, not an industry classifier. Second, network linkage collapses after 2021 (2022 = 2,101 rows). Third, the member link is circular by construction. One more thing is not recorded in any note: Paul's own rebuild uses the naive filing-year Congress rule for unsuffixed citations, which is exactly what this paper warns against.

extraction.research_question: Can network centrality computed from co-voting records (correlations between members' voting records) identify the actual cue-provider or leader in a legislature, and in particular does a proposed absolute-value centrality measure separate cue-providers from followers and majoritarians where the traditional centrality approach cannot? (Inferred from the appendix; the main question is stated in the published article, which is not in this text.)
extraction.theory: Leader or cue-provider theory: a leader whose followers vote with her some percentage of the time (ally followers, opponent followers, or others at other rates). The appendix argues the leader should have the highest network centrality in a co-voting network built from phi correlations of voting records (lines 318-353). Majoritarians are members who vote with the majority; the traditional centrality approach can rank majoritarians above the actual cue-provider (Figure 4 text, line 303).
extraction.data: Empirical data (Table 1, line 12-120): 940 MEP observations (centrality N = 897 after network construction; left-right distance to EP median N = 868; pro/anti-EU distance to EP median N = 872). Unit is the MEP. Variables include centrality (mean .283, SD .138, range .006-.502), party leader (mean .05), committee leader (.09), EP leader (.03), coordinator (.23), reports drafted (mean 1.05), reports amended (6.73), opinions (.72), motions (6.82), speeches (29.07), questions (20.07), declarations (.58), tenure (1.58), party size (172.01), female (.30). Period of the European Parliament data is not stated in the appendix text. Simulated data (Figures 1-6, lines 289-313): 1000 simulated networks per network class (simple, moderate, complex); 1000 simulations; 100 legislators; 1000 rounds of voting in the Figure 5 runs. Figure 6 uses three parameterizations: US (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 40 allies, 40 opponents, 20 others at 50%), Supermajority (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 67 allies, 33 opponents), and EP (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 37 allies, 25 opponents, 38 others at varied rates, roughly the seven-party EP seat allotment).
extraction.method: Centrality is built from pairwise phi correlations of binary voting records (Table 1 is the 2x2 contingency table underlying phi, lines 331-341). The appendix uses an absolute-value version of this centrality, referred to as the "posterior" measure, which is compared with the traditional (signed) centrality calculation. Analytic method: Hypothesis 1 (leader centrality >= follower centrality) is proved algebraically for a three-voter legislature (leader plus two followers) with follow probabilities q2 and q3 and leader Yes-probability p; the condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1 (lines 319-345). The result is extended to n voters by a term-by-term comparison, arguing that each phi term depends only on p and the relevant follow probabilities, so it is unchanged as voters are added (lines 347-353). Simulation method: Monte Carlo generation of cueing networks in three complexity classes, computing the posterior centrality from simulated voting records and correlating it with betweenness, closeness, and weighted degree (Figure 5); and t-tests of cue-provider centrality against the maximum follower and a majoritarian across rounds of voting (Figure 6). Figures 1-4 show cue-provider centrality as a function of follow probabilities.
extraction.scope: Population: members of the European Parliament (party groups named in Table 2: EPP, EPP-ED, PES, ALDE, G/EFA, EUL/NGL, IND/DEM, UEN), plus stylized simulated legislatures (US, supermajority, and EP-style). Institution: European Parliament (empirical) and abstract legislatures (theory). Era: not stated in the appendix text. The theoretical result is stated for single-party legislatures under the stated assumptions.

key_findings.finding: Under the assumptions, in a three-voter legislature the leader's centrality is greater than or equal to each follower's centrality; the condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1, which hold by inspection.
key_findings.location: Complete Proof of Leader Centrality, Hypothesis 1 proof (lines 318-345)
key_findings.numbers: Conditions: q2 < 1 and q3 < 1 (follow probabilities are probabilities).

key_findings.finding: The three-voter result is extended to n voters for the single-party case: the cue-provider has greater or equal centrality than any follower regardless of exogenous parameter values. The text states 'greater' for n = 4 but the inequalities derived are weak (>=).
key_findings.numbers: Proof given for 3, 4, and arbitrary n voters.

key_findings.finding: Posterior absolute-value centrality recovers the true network centralities of simulated cueing networks; it is highly correlated with closeness and weighted degree even in complex networks, and only weakly correlated with betweenness.
key_findings.numbers: Betweenness correlation about 0.25; closeness and weighted degree described as 'highly correlated' (no coefficient reported); 1000 simulations, 100 legislators, 1000 rounds of voting; 1000 networks per class.

key_findings.finding: Simple networks are recovered most accurately; moderate and complex networks less so, because network structure is lost when networks are converted to voting data.
key_findings.numbers: No coefficients reported by class.

key_findings.finding: Cue-provider centrality is significantly higher than the maximum follower and the majoritarian; significance grows with the number of voting rounds, and is described as comparable to available EP data at 1,000 rounds.
key_findings.numbers: Three parameterizations (US, Supermajority, EP); t-scores are described as significant but no t-values are given in the text.

key_findings.finding: With allies and opponents following at 65% and 35%, cue-provider centrality is clearly higher than majoritarians and followers across the 35%-65% range, though the gap is less pronounced than at 80%/20%.
key_findings.numbers: Parameterization 65%/35% versus 80%/20% in the published article.

key_findings.finding: With allies at 80% and opponents at 35%, the absolute-value centrality yields systematically higher cue-provider centrality, while the traditional approach cannot distinguish the cue-providers.
key_findings.numbers: Allies 80%, opponents 35%.

key_findings.finding: With a third group following at 35%, the traditional calculation makes majoritarians systematically more central than the actual cue-provider; the absolute-value measure corrects this.
key_findings.numbers: Allies 80%, opponents 20%, others 35%.

key_findings.finding: Cue-provider centrality is maximized when follow probabilities approach 0 or 1 and minimized when both are 50%.
key_findings.numbers: Follow probabilities on the x and y axes; minimum at (50%, 50%).

key_findings.finding: Descriptive: the top-ranked MEP overall is Braghetto (EPP) at centrality 0.5019; the top 17 are from the EPP; the 18th is Sakalas (PES) at 0.475. Group leaders: PES Sakalas 0.475; ALDE Duff 0.4441; G/EFA Onesta 0.2046; EUL/NGL Svensson 0.1737; IND/DEM Wojciechowski 0.3248; UEN Masiel 0.3893.
key_findings.numbers: Overall mean centrality .283 (Table 1); EPP-ED block lists 5 ranks with the second entry labelled '5' (apparent labeling error in the table, lines 157-171).

limitations: Results are described as highly dependent on parameterization; three sample parameterizations are used (lines 309).
Betweenness centrality correlates only about 0.25 with the posterior measure, so the measure does not recover betweenness well (line 308).
Moderate and complex cueing networks lose network structure when converted to voting data, reducing recovery accuracy (line 308).

summary_md:
This is the online appendix to Ringe and Wilson's paper on co-voting centrality. It holds a proof, simulations and descriptive tables from the European Parliament. The authors build a network from pairwise phi correlations of members' binary voting records. They score each member by an absolute-value (sign-blind) centrality: a member followed reliably by allies (positive phi) or reliably opposed by opponents (negative phi) both count toward that member's centrality.

**Proof.** For a single-party legislature, they show the leader's centrality is at least as high as any follower's. The condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1. The inequalities are weak (greater than or equal), although the n-voter text says "greater".

**Simulations.** There were 1,000 networks per complexity class, with 100 legislators and 1,000 voting rounds.
- The absolute-value measure separates the cue-provider from followers and from "majoritarians" (members who usually vote with the majority).
- The traditional signed measure can rank majoritarians above the true cue-provider when a third group follows at 35% (Figure 4).
- The measure correlates highly with closeness and weighted degree (no coefficient reported), but only about 0.25 with betweenness.
- Moderate and complex networks lose structure when converted to voting data.
- The authors say the results are "highly dependent on parameterization".

**Empirical side.** The data cover 897 MEPs with centrality scores (mean .283). The parliamentary term is not stated in the appendix.

**Why it matters here.**
- Melange has one co-voting layer: the signed vote backbone in the Draft Systems R script, plus its party-controlled Option C. That layer found the raw signed backbone was about 95% party, then dropped the negative side. The paper offers a mechanism for the first finding (the signed measure rewards majoritarians) and an argument against the second (negative ties carry cue-provider information).
- The paper also clarifies the June 2026 retirement of cosponsor centrality from the Influence pillar. The paper treats sign-blindness as a property of a leadership measure, not as a flaw. That supports the system's two-axis rule, which keeps influence and alignment as separate axes.
- None of this transfers directly. The evidence is analytic and simulated, with European Parliament data, and it concerns co-voting, not cosponsorship.

bearings.paper_claim: Signed (traditional) co-voting centrality cannot separate the cue-provider from majoritarians; with a third group following at 35 percent it makes majoritarians systematically more central than the actual cue-provider. The absolute-value measure corrects this. In simulation, cue-provider centrality is lowest when both follow probabilities are 50 percent and highest as they approach 0 or 1.

summary_md:
An unsigned internal memo dated 12/10/2025. Names are redacted and it is not peer-reviewed. It profiles federal political giving by the top 10 firms by revenue in four industries: life insurance, mutual funds, credit unions and commercial banking. It splits that giving across CEOs, other executives, company PACs, trade associations (ACLI, ACU, ABA) and the four largest Super PACs. Its headline claim is that firms push political spending onto executives and adjust their giving to executive-branch scrutiny "regardless of party". The evidence is per-industry dollar averages, which carry no cycle years, source or N, plus news-driven case stories: Bank of America after the DOJ probe, JPMorgan's PAC memos, and the Schwab charity fund. There is no comparison group and no test. The memo reports its own ranking contradictions, and it uses "dark money" to mean Super PAC money.

For Paul's systems the memo is a descriptive input, not evidence. Its unit of analysis is the same one Mentat's spending-statistics sheet already builds. That sheet has role tiers (Chief, Middle Management, Employee, Corporate) and channel columns (Super PAC, Company PAC, Trade Association, Candidate, Company PAC to Super PAC, each with a partisan split). Mentat also ingests a "Credit Union Cross Industry Spending.xlsx" template. The memo may therefore come from the same product line, and if it does it is not an independent check. Two parts are useful. First, the bank, mutual-fund and CU stories show giving moving into channels that per-member models never see: trade associations, Super PACs, and family or charity vehicles. That bears on how Melange's flip model measures competitor money. Second, its partisan readings of Super PAC money ignore whether the money supported or opposed a candidate, which Mentat already separates. Every figure in the memo should be treated as UNVERIFIED, with no window or denominator.

extraction.research_question: Does out-group cueing from Democratic elites, delivered through news coverage, drive the rise of climate skepticism in the US public, especially among Republicans, and can that effect be shown to be causal rather than a by-product of confounders?
extraction.theory: Elite cueing and out-group backlash. Partisans use party elites as cognitive shortcuts and affective anchors (Cohen 2003; Kam 2005; Lenz 2012; Lodge and Taber 2013). Out-group cues can repel rather than persuade partisans, plausibly via affective polarization (Iyengar et al. 2012). The authors contrast this with motivated-reasoning and ideology accounts, which they say cannot easily explain the over-time dynamics, since Republicans once matched Democrats on climate beliefs. News media carry elite cues to the mass public (pp. 2-6). Hypotheses: H1, Democratic elite cues lead aggregate skepticism; H2, a positive contemporaneous correlation holds after controls; H3, exposure to a Democratic cue raises skepticism among Republicans (pp. 5-8).
extraction.data: Aggregate opinion: about 172 Roper Center poll questions (the abstract says "nearly 200 polls") combined into a latent skepticism index. Quarterly 2001-2014 (N=55 in Table 2 Model 1; N=54 for the Republican series) and annual 1986-2014 (N=28). Republican-only series is the Partisan Climate Change Threat Index of Carmichael and Brulle, reverse-coded (correlation 0.48 with the authors' quarterly series). News: climate coverage in the New York Times and Washington Post (LexisNexis), with 1,000+ articles hand-screened for relevance. Validation: 700 party-referencing articles (about 80% contain a cue); 3,000 articles coded for stance (97% of Democratic-cue articles fully pro-consensus); 2,179 newspaper articles coded for economic-cost and uncertainty frames (classifier training sets of 1,878 and 1,179). Experiment: MTurk, 2019, N=2,970 analysed (condition sizes 471-534), with 85% passing screeners and 130 (4%) dropped for failing both (p. 19 and fn 10).
extraction.method: Text-as-data pipeline: Lexicoder plus a custom dictionary of party names, office titles and leaders to flag elite cues. Share of articles with Democratic cues and Republican cues. Republican cue measure is the cue share multiplied by the share of hostile Republican messages (validated against LCV scores, r=0.72). Frames via SVM (80% accuracy for cost frames, recall 0.76 and precision 0.80; 77% accuracy for uncertainty frames, recall 0.70 and precision 0.68). Time series: reduced-form VAR with lags up to four quarters (higher lag chosen when tests disagree; stability checked) and Granger causality tests, with controls for NOAA climate index, oil prices, unemployment and quarter dummies (pp. 11-13). Contemporaneous models: lagged-dependent-variable OLS with robust SEs (Eq. 1), controls for Republican cues, uncertainty and cost frames, salience (NYT plus WaPo volume), climate, oil, unemployment (Table 2). Experiment: OLS (Eq. 2) interacting five treatment dummies (Democratic cue; opposing GOP cue; polarized cues; supporting GOP cue; consensus cues) with 7-point partisanship and with controls (trust in scientists, political interest) and their interactions with treatment. Outcome is a 7-point agree/disagree item on human-caused warming, rescaled 0-1 (pp. 18-21).
extraction.identification: Time series: Granger tests establish temporal precedence only, and the authors state the design is not causal (pp. 6, 12, 17). Contemporaneous models add controls for in-group cues, frames, salience, and lagged skepticism, but remain observational. Experiment: random assignment to six conditions (control; Democratic cue; opposing GOP cue; polarized; supporting GOP cue; consensus), so the cue effect is identified within the randomized conditions. Partisanship is not randomized and enters as a moderator (p. 19). The effects reported are conditional on strong partisanship. Effects are estimated through the PID-by-treatment interaction, not a simple randomized mean difference.
extraction.scope: Population: US public (aggregate polls) and a US online MTurk sample (2019) that the authors say matches the public on gender, race, partisanship and ideology but skews younger, wealthier and more educated (p. 18). Institution: national newspaper coverage (NYT and WaPo) only. Era: 1986-2014 for annual opinion and 2001-2014 for quarterly series; experiment in 2019. Issue: climate change science and mitigation.

limitations: VAR and Granger analyses cannot speak to contemporaneous relationships or causality; authors say so (pp. 6, 12, 16).
Aggregate evidence is described as only suggestive; unmeasured confounders over time remain (p. 17).
Results are sensitive to lag length; the authors pick the higher lag when tests disagree and note the sensitivity (fn 6, p. 12).
Small time series (N=28 annual, 54-55 quarterly) with many controls.
Cue measure is a share of articles from dictionary-based classification, not message volume; volume robustness is only in supplementary Table D1 (p. 10).

Republican hostility measure is a composite built from a 3,000-article coding and an LCV correlation (0.72); the authors call the stance indicator valid but it is not directly measured for every period (pp. 10-11).
Only NYT and WaPo are used; the authors acknowledge partisan online and social media are excluded (fn 3, p. 9).
Inconsistent counts: the abstract says nearly 200 polls, the body uses 172 poll questions (p. 8). The abstract says about 3,000 respondents; 2,970 were analysed.
Experimental sample is MTurk, skewing younger, wealthier and more educated; screeners address bot and VPN concerns (pp. 18-19, fn 10).
Partisanship is not randomized; treatment effects are moderated by PID, which may carry confounding (p. 19).
No effect among Democrats, possibly from a ceiling effect (p. 22).
Treatments are thin and the outcome is a single 7-point item (pp. 18-21).
Consensus cue did not depolarize; the authors suggest a stronger treatment from respected Republicans may be needed (p. 23).
Table 2 layout is hard to read: the text reports Model 1 Republican cues as non-significant, while the table marks Dem cues only with stars; p-values are reported as approximate (p~).

summary_md:
Merkley and Stecula ask whether climate skepticism in the US public grew because people reacted against Democratic elites, with news coverage carrying those cues. They combine three methods. First, a Lexicoder dictionary flags party cues in NYT and WaPo climate coverage. Second, they run time-series models on a latent skepticism index built from about 172 poll questions. Third, they run a 2019 MTurk experiment with N=2,970.

In the time series, the share of articles carrying Democratic cues Granger-causes skepticism, both in the aggregate (chi2 6.96, p=0.01) and among Republicans (chi2 7.35, p=0.03). The reverse direction does not hold. Republican cues have no aggregate effect (p=0.94). In the experiment, a single Democratic cue moves strong Republicans +0.06 toward skepticism on a 0-1 scale (about 0.2 SD). A polarized cue, Democrats for and Republicans against, moves them +0.09. A consensus cue, with Republicans joining Democrats, produces no movement and does not depolarize. More coverage alone, with cues held fixed, goes with lower Republican skepticism (-0.4 SD per +100 articles a quarter). The Granger tests show only which series moves first, not causation. The causal evidence is one MTurk experiment on mass partisans, not legislators.

For Melange, the paper's value is about direction. An out-party cue is not a weaker positive cue. Among mass partisans it pushes the other way. Three parts of the engine encode out-party cues differently:
- The cascade kernel's cpf_pressure gives an out-party source 0.5x pull, a weaker push in the same direction.
- The LT-priming cross-cue is clamped at 0 and never goes negative.
- The salience shock already has a Retreat regime that moves out-partisans -1, but its Rally regime still gives bridge-builders +0.5. The paper's consensus condition found no movement at all.

The paper does not supply a legislator-level backfire magnitude. Every transfer runs from the mass public to members of Congress and from climate to credit-union issues, so any recalibration is UNVERIFIED and remains Paul's decision.

bearings.paper_claim: A polarized cue (Democrats for, Republicans against) moves strong Republicans +0.09 points on the 0-1 scale (about 0.3 SD, p~0.002). It is numerically the largest cue effect, but the authors do not report it as significantly different from the single Democratic cue or opposing-GOP cue effects. A single Democratic cue moves them +0.06 (p~0.03). Supporting-GOP and consensus cues show no polarizing effect and no de-polarizing effect. Observationally, +100 articles a quarter with cues held fixed goes with -0.4 SD in Republican skepticism (Model 3, PCCTI, N=54; p~0.03).
bearings.paper_location: Experimental results and Figure 3 Panels A-C, pp. 20-21; Table 2 Model 3, p. 17; discussion pp. 22-23
bearings.system_side: Going public is three regimes. Retreat moves co-partisans +1 and out-partisans -1, matching the paper's polarized-cue backlash direction. Rally moves out-partisans +0.5 only when bpf is at least 0.30, which the paper's consensus null does not support. Regime probabilities p and q come from the D-R tier gap z in salience_issue_params, and the advisory actor party defaults to R.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over only as a direction-of-effect prior. The paper studies mass partisans reacting to elite cues in national newspapers on climate; the engine moves legislators' stance tiers on credit-union issues. The rally result rests on one thin MTurk treatment, so it weakens but does not refute out-partisan rally movement. Treating z as endogenous to going public is the analyst's inference, not the paper's; the Granger results concern cue shares and skepticism, not the partisan stance gap.
bearings.verifier_note: Numbers, panels, pages and the Retreat/Rally code verified at the cited lines. Softened: 'largest effect' should read numerically largest, since no significant difference is reported; 'no movement at all' overstates the consensus null. The claim that z is a snapshot the campaign never changes was not verified.

bearings.system_side: The Bakker cross-cue factor xf passes a cross-party pro-cue through sqrt(bpf_u*bpf_v), so a non-bridge out-party cue falls to about 0. The priming term is clamped at 0 and never goes negative; the code comment says backfire magnitude is not invented.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports that out-party cues do not persuade and reads as backlash, so a negative sign is consistent with it. But the +0.06 effect is measured on mass Republicans and one climate item, not on legislators reading cosponsorship signals, so it cannot set a backfire magnitude for the priming term. Keeping the zero clamp remains defensible.
bearings.verifier_note: All numbers and pages match the text and Table 1. The clamp and cross-cue factor are confirmed at the cited lines. The paper does not itself say the sign can be negative; that is the bearing's reading of 'repelled, rather than persuaded' (p. 17).

bearings.paper_claim: Democratic cues move Republicans toward skepticism, away from the cued position, in both the experiment and the time series (backlash rather than attenuated persuasion). Republican cues have no aggregate effect (chi2 0.00, p=0.94) and only a weak effect on Republican skepticism (chi2 2.94, p~0.09). The authors say co-partisan sources dominate.
bearings.paper_location: Table 1, p. 15; Figure 3, p. 20; discussion p. 22
bearings.system_side: cpf_pressure gives an out-partisan source a 0.5x pull and a co-partisan source 1.7x; cpf_diffusion keeps a 0.4 cross-party floor. Both keep out-party influence positive and weaker, not negative.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports co-partisan sources dominating, which fits the 1.7 versus 0.5 ordering. It reports backlash, meaning movement away from the cued position, but estimates no multiplier relative to co-partisan influence, so it cannot show the out-partisan sign should be at or below zero rather than 0.5. Cosponsorship ties are observed behaviour rather than cues, so transfer is weak. The paper gives no support for the 1.7/0.5 ratio itself.
bearings.verifier_note: Table 1 numbers verified. The original bearing used Republican cues, which are in-party for Republicans, as evidence of out-party backlash; the paper_claim is rewritten to attribute backlash to Democratic cues. Code lines verified. The 'at or below zero' reading is the analyst's extrapolation, not the paper's estimate.

bearings.paper_claim: The authors use Lexicoder with a custom dictionary of party names, office titles and party leaders to detect party cues, not sentiment or tone. They validate detection against hand coding of a random 700 articles (about 80% contain a cue by their definition). Stance is hand-coded on a separate random sample of 3000 articles (97% of articles with Democratic messages are wholly pro-consensus). Frames come from SVM classifiers (77-80% accuracy).

Live run_stage5.R defaults the intensity to the absolute net tone per word (INTENSITY default net_norm, line 45), with charge only as an option, and press_value equals final_sign times that intensity at lines 141-143. The bearing's earlier statement that charge per word is the intensity used in press_value was wrong.

The system_side and code_ref were wrong: the live default intensity is net tone per word, not charge, and press_value is computed in run_stage5.R, not stage5_lsd.R.

summary_issues: Consensus cue wording overstates the null: summary says it 'produces no movement and does not depolarize'; the paper reports no polarizing effect and no de-polarizing effect found for the consensus and supporting-GOP conditions (pp. 21-23).

Summary says 'the paper's consensus condition found no movement at all'; the paper reports no polarizing effect, not zero movement, and the Democratic-cue effect is described as attenuated by the supporting GOP cue (p. 21).
Summary calls the Rally regime's +0.5 'bridge-builders'; the code gives +0.5 to out-partisans whose bpf is at least 0.30 (cross-pressured out-partisans, salience_shock.py:99-111).
The -0.4 SD per +100 articles a quarter figure comes from Model 3 (Republican skepticism, PCCTI, N=54), not aggregate skepticism; the summary should say so.

Summary is otherwise accurate on the Granger statistics (6.96/0.01; 7.35/0.03; reverse 0.32 and 0.86; GOP cues 0.00/0.94), the experiment effects (+0.06 single cue, +0.09 polarized, about 0.2 and 0.3 SD), N=2,970, 172 poll questions, and the 2019 MTurk design.
Paul's highlight claims in paul_alignment were not checked against the annotation file (_annots/049ac0d19237.json); they are outside summary_md but the alignment text is unverified.
The LSD bearing's system_side and code_ref were corrected in this verification (default intensity is net tone per word; press_value is in run_stage5.R).
gaps_exposed: The engine never lets a source's party identity produce a negative cue. The cascade kernel, LT priming and the rally regime all keep out-party influence at zero or above. The only negative out-party movement is the salience shock's Retreat and Backfire regimes, and it never feeds the cascade kernel.

The salience shock takes partisan polarization (z) as a fixed snapshot of the stance matrix. Nothing models a CU campaign led by one party creating or widening the partisan gap over later quarters, which is the dynamic the Granger results describe.

Message attribution, meaning which party's elites are seen as owning a CU issue in press and news, is not measured. The frame-alignment and press layers measure duplication and stance, not attribution of party cues in third-party coverage.
The salience shock has no consensus regime. The paper's consensus condition (both parties supportive) is a distinct case with a null effect, not a rally that moves out-partisans +0.5.
flags: The paper's aggregate contemporaneous coefficient (0.02, p~0.07 quarterly; p~0.09 annual) pools Democrats and Republicans across the partisan fault line the paper is about. If quoted, label it UNSTRATIFIED and pair it with the Republican-only Model 3 (0.03, p<0.01, N=54, quarterly 2001-2014).
The Granger results depend on lag choice (the authors take the higher lag when tests disagree, fn 6). Quote them as evidence of which series moves first, never as causal.

Any proposal to give out-partisan pressure a negative sign, or to set a backfire magnitude in lt_priming, from the +0.06 or +0.09 MTurk effects would be new agent analysis, UNVERIFIED (DE-062). Those effects are mass-public climate effects and say nothing about legislators.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals, D-021 or D-025. The paper argues for neither dropping cosponsorship edges nor per-edge volume normalization.
paul_alignment: Paul's highlights match the paper's core claim (Democratic cues, Republican backlash, consensus cues fail). His component notes list Merkley and Stecula as support for treating party as a filter on receptiveness (cascade kernel) and as a companion to Noble and Turner (salience shock). The evidence agrees on direction but is stronger than the system as built. The paper finds that out-party cues backfire. In the code, out-party influence is attenuated but positive in cpf_pressure and the rally regime, and clamped at 0 in LT priming. So Paul's note is consistent with the system but understates the gap: the system handles backfire only through the salience shock's Retreat and Backfire regimes. His highlight of the Lexicoder method under lsd-tone is a loose fit. The paper used Lexicoder to detect party actors, not to measure tone, so it does not validate the LSD intensity the system uses. His closing highlights on cross-partisan elite consensus are tempered by the paper's own null for the consensus condition.

related.why: Noble and Turner's item covers going-public structure (Prop. 1, p. 13: going public widens the gridlock region), which the salience shock implements. Merkley and Stecula give mass-public evidence that the out-partisan retreat direction is real (polarized-cue backlash). Their consensus null is not a test of Noble's rally regime, so it does not show a rally fails to move out-partisans.

Bakker et al. (Study 1: out-party cue -0.06 on a 0-1 scale, p<.01) is the cited basis for the LT-priming cross-cue clamp. Merkley and Stecula independently find out-party cues move Republicans against the cue, on climate and in news coverage.

Box-Steffensmeier et al. study legislators taking cues from interest-group Dear Colleague letters; Merkley and Stecula study the mass public taking cues from party elites in news. Together they mark the legislator versus voter boundary for cue parameters.

Rice and Zorn's item shows corpus-based dictionaries beat standard ones (LIWC, AFINN) on specialized vocabulary, which bears on applying LSD2015 to congressional releases. Merkley and Stecula use Lexicoder with a custom party-cue dictionary validated against hand coding.

Haselmayer and Jenny pair a dictionary with crowdcoding validation (480 coders, 92% mean accuracy). Merkley and Stecula pair a dictionary with hand-coded validation of 700 articles. Whether the LSD tone layer has an equivalent validation sample was not checked (validate_stage5.R was not read).

backlinks.why: Merkley and Stecula show outgroup backlash to overt partisan elite cues in news. This paper explains why senders facing mixed audiences shift to covert cues to avoid that backlash.

Uses Lexicoder plus a custom dictionary of party names and leaders to detect party cues, not sentiment, and validates that dictionary against hand-coded articles. Verified in the Merkley item; the link is about dictionary practice, not about tone measurement.

extraction.coverage: Full text read: all of _text/995e0e0b27e3.txt (lines 0-660, PDF pages 1551-1556, including abstract, introduction, related work, method, simulation results, conclusion and references). Metadata hint corrected: authors are Qingli Zeng and Farid Nait-Abdesselam (both University of Missouri-Kansas City); venue is IEEE ICC 2024; DOI is in the text. No Paul markup files existed (none), so paul_markup is empty. Content check: the paper contains no lobbying, legislators, elections, persuasion/turnout, allocation, text-measurement or social-network material. The only network-like element is distance-based neighbour interaction among drones. Those topics are therefore absent, not thin. The paper's own references to networks are to UAV communication surveys, not social networks.
extraction.research_question: Can drones trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning (Q-learning with function approximation) reproduce bird-flock behaviour (cohesion, alignment, separation, following) more adaptively than rule-based Boid models? The text states the aim as this comparison rather than as a formal question.
extraction.theory: Reynolds' Boid model (cohesion, separation, alignment) extended with a leader-follow rule and connectivity band, with reinforcement learning as the adaptive mechanism. Framework is an MDP tuple (S, A, P, R) solved by Q-learning, with linear Q-value approximation Q(s,a)=w·phi(s,a) and Bellman updates (Eqs. 2-6). Rewards are the sum of four terms (Eqs. 7-14).
extraction.data: No empirical data. Simulated drone swarm built in Python with Pygame. Unit: UAV (drone). Sample: N = 17 UAVs in the simulation parameters (Table I); training uses three designated UAVs (V1 leader on a predefined trajectory, V2 follower, V3 learner). Period: 3,500 simulation steps per method (Table II). Working area 600 x 800 units, maximum speed 4, distance thresholds d1=20, d2=40, d3=80 (Table I). Number of independent runs and random seeds are not reported.
extraction.method: Simulation comparison of two controllers: (a) Q-learning/MARL-trained drones with linear function approximation (learning rate initialised at alpha=0.1 and said to adapt across iterations; discount gamma=0.75) and (b) a rule-based Boid baseline. Reward weights from Table I: collision -20, connectivity +1, alignment with leader +5 (closer) and -1 (farther), cohesion +2. Sequential training: follower V2 learns to trail the leader at about 30 units; learner V3 learns to trail V1 while staying near V2 and avoiding collisions. Performance is reported as four counts or averages over the run: proximity advances, ideal-range tracking (20-40 units), near-collision events (within 20 units), and heading consistency (mean heading-angle difference, Eqs. 15-16). The rule-based baseline is not specified in the text beyond being a Boid-type rule model.
extraction.identification: None. The comparison is a single descriptive contrast of two controllers on one simulated scenario. No statistical test, confidence interval, replication, or ablation is reported.
extraction.scope: Population: simulated drones in a 2D Pygame environment (dimensionality is implied by the working-area dimensions but not stated). Institution: University of Missouri-Kansas City. Era: 2024. Results apply only to the single simulated scenario in Table I.

key_findings.finding: Abstract claims the MARL Boid surpasses rule-based models in cohesion, alignment and separation, and shows robustness to perturbations. Section IV reports only the Table II comparison; no perturbation experiment is reported in the text.
key_findings.numbers: Not applicable (qualitative claim)

key_findings.finding: Both methods completed the task over the same horizon.
key_findings.numbers: Steps 3,500 for RL and rule-based

key_findings.finding: RL drones recorded more proximity advances than rule-based drones.
RL drones spent more instances within the ideal 20-40 unit range.
RL drones had far fewer near-collision events, which the authors read as improved safety.
key_findings.location: Table II and text, Section IV-B, p.1556

key_findings.finding: RL heading consistency is reported as better (lower average heading deviation, assuming the metric is a deviation, as defined on p.1556).

Conclusion: RL can minimise collisions, keep consistent headings and keep proximity, and may suit dynamic scenarios that hard-coded rules handle poorly. These are the authors' interpretations of the single comparison, not tested in the text.

summary_md:
Zeng and Nait-Abdesselam (IEEE ICC 2024) train simulated drones with Q-learning and linear function approximation to reproduce Reynolds' Boid flocking rules: cohesion, alignment and separation, plus a leader-follow rule and a connectivity band. They compare this controller with an unspecified rule-based Boid baseline. The setup is one Pygame scenario with 17 UAVs and 3,500 steps. Training is sequential: one leader, one follower and one learner. Reward weights are fixed by hand (collision -20, alignment +5/-1, cohesion +2, connectivity +1).

Table II favours the RL controller on every count:
- proximity advances: 2,097 vs 1,976
- steps within the 20-40 unit ideal range: 3,176 vs 2,764
- near-collision events: 45 vs 108
- mean heading deviation: 14.3 vs 21.1

The evidence is thin. There is one scenario, with no seeds, replicates, variance or test. The baseline is never described. The counts are not normalised for swarm size. The abstract claims robustness to perturbations, but no perturbation experiment is reported.

For Paul's systems the paper is essentially out of scope. It contains no legislators, lobbying, money, text, elections or social-network structure. Its only network-like element is distance-based neighbour interaction among physical agents. The one thin link is methodological. It is another case of a learned policy beating a hand-set rule baseline, which is the kind of claim Paul's notes make when they expect GCOMB or contingency-aware RL to replace greedy allocation. On its own evidence the paper cannot support that expectation. A single uncontrolled, unreplicated comparison would not pass the project's single-look discipline, so it should be read only as an example of the claim type. It is not evidence for it. No component's assumptions, constants or code paths are tested, supported or contradicted by this work.

bearings.paper_claim: An RL controller (Q-learning, linear function approximation, alpha 0.1, gamma 0.75) beats a rule-based Boid baseline on one simulated drone scenario: near-collisions 45 vs 108 (-58%), ideal-range steps 3,176 vs 2,764 (+15%), heading deviation 14.3 vs 21.1, all over 3,500 steps with N = 17 UAVs. No seeds, replicates, variance or baseline specification are given.
bearings.paper_location: Table I (p.1555) and Table II with Section IV-B (p.1556)
bearings.system_side: The built optimizer uses deterministic CELF lazy greedy over per-member concave chunks ($500 steps, PMAX $10k cap, stance-gated members excluded). It has no learned policy. Paul's notes expect a learned policy (GCOMB) to replace greedy at scale.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over only as an analogy: a learned policy versus hand-set rules in a multi-agent setting. Nothing transfers to political allocation. The agents are physical drones, the reward is hand-specified geometry, and there is no budget, submodularity, money or legislator response. The evidence is one unreplicated simulation, so it cannot show that RL would outperform greedy anywhere, let alone on the cosponsor kernel.

gaps_exposed: None specific to the system. The paper's topic (drone swarm control) is absent from every component. The only general point is a reminder: if a learned allocation or seeding policy (GCOMB, contingency-aware RL) is ever built, its comparison with CELF greedy needs replicates, seeds and a fully specified baseline. This paper provides none of the three.
flags: Out of scope: the paper contains no lobbying, legislators, elections, persuasion, money, text-measurement or social-network material. Do not cite it as support for any Melange component.

Its RL-beats-rules claim rests on a single unreplicated simulation with no reported variance, and the robustness claim in the abstract has no experiment behind it. If it is ever cited for 'learned policies beat greedy/rule baselines', label the claim UNVERIFIED in line with the project's single-look and DE-062 standards.
Its distance-based neighbour interaction is not a social tie. It should not be read as support for neighbour-based stance imputation or cascade edges, whose co-movement test was null in this project.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation of this paper, and none of his component positions cite it. Its one point of contact is his expectation that a learned policy (GCOMB, Chen et al. 2021 contingency-aware RL) will eventually replace greedy allocation and seeding. The paper repeats the general claim that RL beats hand-set rules, but on evidence too thin to strengthen that expectation. It neither confirms nor dates any of his notes. The system as built (CELF greedy, the SGATE table) is unaffected.

related.why: Both use reinforcement learning to replace a hand-set rule policy. Chen et al. do it for seeding legislators-as-nodes under take-up uncertainty, which is the literature actually behind the SGATE seed gate. Zeng applies RL only to physical swarm control.

Same UAV application domain. Luo plans paths for single drones with D* Lite, while Zeng controls a swarm with RL. Both are engineering simulations relevant to Paul's pathfinding reading only by analogy.
